paperInfo.paperName: Grade 7 Social Science — Paper 2 (Practice Set B - Structured Heritage & Social Studies)

questions.questionText: A local market has become untidy after a busy trading day. Your class is preparing a display about Zimbabwean heritage. The teacher asks learners to identify physical evidence from the past and explain why it should be protected. a) Name one example of a heritage site or artefact that could be included.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** A strong Grade 7 Heritage Studies answer set around a busy local community market is **Great Zimbabwe National Monument** near Masvingo (dry-stone granite walls built by ancestral Shona builders without mortar) or the **carved Soapstone Zimbabwe Birds (Hungwe)** discovered at Great Zimbabwe. Other fully accepted Zimbabwean examples include **Khami Ruins**, **Domboshava / Matobo Hills rock paintings** by the San people, or the **mbira dzavadzimu** traditional musical instrument.

Heritage sites and cultural artefacts serve as living physical archives proving the engineering mastery, governance, trade networks, and spiritual artistry of earlier Zimbabwean generations long before colonial arrival. Including photographs, clay models, or sketched replicas of stone walls and the soapstone bird in a class display allows learners and visiting parents to connect textbook history with real national emblems appearing on Zimbabwe’s flag and currency.

ZIMSEC General Paper 2 markers expect a specific named Zimbabwean monument or genuine cultural object rather than a vague noun like "an old building" or "stones". Writing a precise example such as **Great Zimbabwe Ruins** or **Soapstone Zimbabwe Bird** together with one brief identifying detail secures full marks cleanly.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, b) State one reason for preserving the item or site.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** One central reason for preserving Great Zimbabwe and related cultural artefacts is that **they safeguard our national identity, history, and ancestral craftsmanship for future generations to study and take pride in**. A closely linked second reason is economic sustainability: well-protected heritage sites attract **cultural and educational tourism**, generating foreign currency and local employment for guides, artisans, and hospitality workers.

Once dry-stone granite walls collapse or ancient San rock paintings fade through vandalism and soot, that irreplaceable primary historical evidence disappears forever—meaning children lose tangible proof of pre-colonial state organisation, iron smelting, and gold trade along the Save and Limpopo valleys. Preserving artefacts also reinforces *Unhu/Ubuntu* respect for elders and national heroes buried or honoured at historic shrines.

In ZIMSEC Grade 7 General Paper, avoid circular phrasing such as *"we keep heritage so it stays nice"*. Link preservation clearly to **preserving cultural history/identity for future generations** or **promoting heritage tourism and education** in a full, grammatically complete sentence.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, c) Explain one way learners can help protect heritage.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** Learners can actively protect heritage sites and artefacts by **practising responsible stewardship when visiting monuments—never climbing ancient dry-stone walls, scratching graffiti onto rock art, or littering around cultural shrines—and reporting damage immediately to site custodians or teachers**. They can also **record oral history stories from village elders and share community heritage awareness campaigns** so peers appreciate why old crafts and sites deserve care.

Youth conservation clubs show how small everyday habits protect national treasures over decades. For example, staying strictly behind marked ropes at Great Zimbabwe prevents loose weathered granite blocks from shifting, while carrying snack wrappers home keeps fragile ecosystems clean around sacred springs and gravesites under traditional taboos (*zviera*).

Examiners reward practical, age-appropriate actions that Grade 7 learners can genuinely perform rather than unrealistic government policies like *"pass an international law"*. Naming one concrete action (no touching fragile rock art / zero littering / educating peers) plus *how it prevents damage* earns full marks.

questions.questionText: A local market has become untidy after a busy trading day. A household has several tasks to complete each Saturday. The family decides to share the work fairly instead of expecting one person to do everything. a) Give one household task that a learner could reasonably perform.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** A safe, age-appropriate household chore that a Grade 7 learner can perform during Saturday clean-up set around a busy local community market is **sweeping the courtyard and living room floor, washing dishes after meals, fetching water in manageable containers, tending vegetable beds, or neatly folding laundry**. Tasks requiring dangerous tools or heavy lifting—such as spraying toxic farm pesticides or splitting thick logs with an adult axe—should remain reserved for adults.

Giving upper-primary learners dependable daily or weekend responsibilities builds practical self-reliance, time management, and pride in contributing to the household alongside academic revision. Under **Unhu/Ubuntu** family upbringing in Zimbabwe, sharing chores teaches young people that every comfortable home depends on everyone’s honest labour rather than gender stereotypes that unfairly dump all cleaning and cooking onto girls alone.

ZIMSEC markers look for realistic, safe chores stated clearly in a full sentence (for example, *"A learner can sweep the yard and wash plates safely"*). Adding why the task suits a Grade 7 child demonstrates mature civic understanding.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, b) State one benefit of sharing household chores.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** Sharing household chores fairly **completes all domestic work much faster and reduces physical exhaustion and stress on any single parent or older sibling**. Instead of one tired family member spending the entire Saturday sweeping, fetching water, and cooking alone, dividing chores proportionally frees time for everyone to rest, attend community meetings, or prepare school homework calmly.

From a life-skills perspective, shared duty distributes practical competence across every child—meaning boys learn cooking and hygiene while girls practise garden carpentry or budgeting—building resilient adults ready for boarding school or future careers. Fairness at home mirrors Zimbabwe’s proverb *"Chara chimwe hachitswanyi inda"* (one thumb alone cannot crush a louse: teamwork achieves what isolated effort struggles to finish).

In General Paper 2, frame benefits specifically around **saving time, reducing fatigue/overload, or teaching equal life skills** rather than generic phrases like *"it is good"*. Stating one clear practical outcome earns full credit immediately.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, c) Explain how fair sharing can improve family relationships.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [3 marks]:** Fair chore distribution strengthens family harmony because **it eliminates resentment, silent bitterness, and frequent quarrels over one member feeling overworked or treated unfairly while others remain idle**. When parents and children plan a transparent rota together and thank one another for finished tasks, mutual respect, trust, and warm cooperation grow naturally across the household.

Psychologically, learners who see their efforts valued feel a deeper sense of belonging and willingness to communicate openly with parents and siblings about school challenges. Conversely, favouritism or dumping heavy chores repeatedly on one child breeds frustration and weakens family unity during times of economic or emotional hardship.

Examiners award maximum marks when candidates explain *both* what fair sharing prevents (resentment/conflict) and what positive bond it builds (mutual respect, unity, and open cooperation). Mentioning **Unhu/Ubuntu family unity** adds strong local curriculum depth.

questions.questionText: A local market has become untidy after a busy trading day. A learner finds a wallet containing money near the school gate. No owner is immediately visible. a) State one value that should guide the learner's decision.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** The foundational moral value that should guide a learner who discovers a lost wallet set around a busy local community market is **honesty** (alongside **integrity** and **empathy / *Unhu/Ubuntu***—doing what is right even when nobody is watching). Honesty requires returning property that belongs to someone else instead of secretly taking advantage of another person’s misfortune.

Within Zimbabwe’s Heritage & Social Science curriculum, *Unhu/Ubuntu* teaches that a person’s dignity is rooted in fairness toward neighbours (*"Munhu munhu nekuda kwevanhu"*). Consider the real hardship losing bus fare, school fees, or medical money inside a wallet causes to a parent or market trader—empathy helps a learner imagine how relieved they would feel if someone returned their own lost belongings.

ZIMSEC marking guides seek an exact named moral virtue such as **honesty** or **integrity** paired with a clear sentence explaining how that virtue applies to unowned property near the school gate. Avoid vague words like *"kindness"* without explicitly naming **honesty/trustworthiness**.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, b) Give one appropriate action the learner should take.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** The correct action is **to leave the wallet’s cash untouched and hand the wallet immediately to a trusted adult in authority—such as the senior teacher on duty, the school headteacher, or a school security guard—while stating exactly where and when it was found** so the school can announce it safely or verify the true owner’s identification before returning it.

Handing lost property straight to the school office creates a transparent witness record protecting the finder against false accusations that money went missing later, while giving the real owner one clear, safe place to enquire. Never walk around displaying loose cash inside the playground or hand the wallet to random strangers who might falsely claim ownership.

In Paper 2 scenario questions, state a **specific, safe chain-of-custody step** (taking it directly to the **headteacher / teacher on duty** or nearest police post) rather than saying *"look around randomly"* or *"keep it until tomorrow"*.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, c) Explain why keeping the wallet would be wrong.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [3 marks]:** Secretly keeping a lost wallet and spending someone else’s money is morally wrong because **it amounts to theft / dishonesty and destroys trust within the school and wider community**, causing severe financial distress to the rightful owner who may have needed that money for food, transport, clinic medicine, or exam fees. Even though no witness saw the learner pick up the wallet, taking property you did not earn violates personal integrity and school rules.

Furthermore, schools and local legal principles distinguish honestly finding lost property from wrongful appropriation (*"theft by finding"*): keeping items when reasonable steps exist to locate the owner via the school office is unlawful and carries disciplinary consequences if discovered later through witnesses or identification cards inside the wallet.

For full marks in ZIMSEC Paper 2 explanations, connect **moral/legal wrongness** (it is dishonest/stealing) directly to **human harm suffered by the victim** and **loss of personal reputation and community trust**.

questions.questionText: A local market has become untidy after a busy trading day. After heavy rain, water collects around a school compound. The health club notices that some containers are holding stagnant water. a) State one health risk associated with stagnant water.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** Standing stagnant water collected in old tyres, open tins, and blocked drains set around a busy local community market creates ideal breeding pools for **female *Anopheles* mosquitoes, sharply increasing the risk of malaria outbreaks** (alongside breeding nuisance **bilharzia** freshwater snails in slow ponds and spreading waterborne diarrhoea germs like **cholera or typhoid** if polluted runoff contaminates drinking wells).

Unlike clean fast-flowing river water, still rainwater traps decaying leaves and warmth, letting mosquito eggs hatch into wriggling larvae and emerge as adult blood-feeding vectors within just 7 to 10 days after summer rains. Children playing outdoors at dusk or sleeping without treated mosquito nets near stagnant compound puddles face severe fever, chills, anaemia, and missed school days.

ZIMSEC markers look for an explicit link between **stagnant water**, the **vector/pathogen** (mosquitoes), and a **named disease** (**malaria**—never confuse malaria with cholera alone unless mentioning dirty drinking water contamination).

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, b) Give one action the school can take immediately.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** The school health club and maintenance team should immediately **drain all puddles and waterlogged drains around the compound, empty and overturn or puncture discarded containers/tins and old tyres so rainwater cannot collect, and clear overgrown tall grass** where adult mosquitoes rest during daytime heat.

Eliminating stagnant breeding habitats at the source cuts adult mosquito populations rapidly across the whole school yard without requiring expensive chemical spraying—a zero-cost intervention every primary school can organise safely using gloves, rakes, and wheelbarrows during afternoon clean-up duty. Covering rainwater storage drums tightly with fine mesh netting prevents mosquitoes laying eggs in useful harvested water too.

Keep answers grounded in **immediate, practical school action** (draining puddles / overturning open containers / unblocking storm drains) rather than slow external steps like *"wait for a hospital team next month"*.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, c) Explain why environmental hygiene is part of disease prevention.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [3 marks]:** **Environmental hygiene**—keeping water clean, disposing of litter safely, maintaining hygienic Blair toilets, and eliminating stagnant breeding sites—is central to disease prevention because **most dangerous community infections rely on dirty physical surroundings to harbour pathogens and disease vectors like flies, mosquitoes, and rats**. Removing filth breaks the chain of transmission *before* microbes ever enter human bodies, preventing entire outbreaks rather than waiting to treat sick patients at clinics later.

Clean water and vector-free surroundings save families clinic fees, prevent missed classroom learning days, and safeguard young children whose immune systems are still developing. When market stalls, school toilets, and village boreholes are kept spotless daily, bacteria such as *Vibrio cholerae* and parasites like *Plasmodium* lose both transport routes and breeding habitats simultaneously.

Examiners reward explanations that clearly show the link **"prevention is better and cheaper than cure"** alongside naming **vectors/pathogens** interrupted by clean sanitation and drainage.

**Model Answer [2 marks]:** Standing stagnant water collected in old tyres, open tins, and blocked drains grounded in preparing a Zimbabwean family farm for the next season creates ideal breeding pools for **female *Anopheles* mosquitoes, sharply increasing the risk of malaria outbreaks** (alongside breeding nuisance **bilharzia** freshwater snails in slow ponds and spreading waterborne diarrhoea germs like **cholera or typhoid** if polluted runoff contaminates drinking wells).

Unlike clean fast-flowing river water, still rainwater traps decaying leaves and warmth, letting mosquito eggs hatch into wriggling larvae and emerge as adult blood-feeding vectors within just 7 to 10 days after summer rains. Children playing outdoors at dusk or sleeping without treated mosquito nets near stagnant compound puddles face severe fever, chills, anaemia, and missed school days.

ZIMSEC markers look for an explicit link between **stagnant water**, the **vector/pathogen** (mosquitoes), and a **named disease** (**malaria**—never confuse malaria with cholera alone unless mentioning dirty drinking water contamination).

questions.questionText: A local market has become untidy after a busy trading day. A community notices that a nearby stream is becoming muddy because vegetation along the banks has been removed. a) Name one environmental problem shown in the situation.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** Clearing grass, reeds, and trees along a stream bank set around a busy local community market directly exposes loose soil to **soil erosion** (specifically riverbank erosion) and consequent **river/dam siltation**, turning the flowing stream muddy brown as heavy rainwater washes unanchored topsoil directly into the watercourse.

Notice how the prompt gives two unmistakable visual clues: *"vegetation along the banks has been removed"* and *"stream is becoming muddy"*. That suspended mud consists of fertile topsoil stripped off nearby gardens or footpaths—reducing agricultural productivity on land while gradually filling local dams and weirs with silt downstream so they hold less water during dry winter months.

State the precise environmental term (**soil erosion** or **siltation / water pollution by eroded soil**) clearly in one sharp opening sentence rather than vague phrasing like *"the water looks bad"*.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, b) State one measure that could protect the stream bank.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** Communities can protect bare stream banks by **replanting indigenous riverine grasses (such as vetiver grass), reeds, and trees along a protected buffer strip—enforcing Zimbabwe’s 30-metre stream-bank cultivation rule—and placing stone gabions or sandbags along eroded gullies** while stopping cattle from trampling fragile wet banks.

Zimbabwe’s Environmental Management Agency (EMA) regulations forbid ploughing gardens right up to river edges precisely because undisturbed 30-metre vegetative buffers act as natural sponges: slowing storm runoff, filtering trapped mud before it enters water, and rebuilding stable habitats for frogs, birds, and fish. Providing separate drinking troughs away from streams keeps livestock hooves from breaking banks down.

In ZIMSEC General Paper 2, citing **replanting stream-bank grasses/trees** or **avoiding stream-bank cultivation (keeping a 30 m buffer)** hits the official environmental studies marking scheme word-for-word.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, c) Explain how vegetation reduces erosion.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [3 marks]:** Vegetation protects soil from erosion through three coordinated natural mechanisms: first, **leaf canopies and stems intercept heavy raindrops**, breaking their downward impact speed so raindrops soak gently into soil instead of splashing loose dirt particles upward. Second, **dense underground plant roots bind soil particles tightly together** like living netting, anchoring stream banks and slopes against rushing water and strong winds.

Third, **fallen leaves and surface grass blades form organic mulch and roughness** that slow surface water runoff speed dramatically, giving rainwater extra time to infiltrate downward into underground water tables instead of carving deep gullies across fields. Keeping natural ground cover intact also nourishes earthworms whose tunnels absorb storm downpours effortlessly.

Examiners award all marks when candidates mention **roots binding soil** AND **leaves cushioning rainfall impact / slowing runoff**, rather than stopping after just *"plants hold dirt"*.

questions.questionText: A local market has become untidy after a busy trading day. A farmer wants to improve crop production on a small field. The soil is losing nutrients and weeds are competing with the crops. a) Name one organic material that could be added to the soil.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** A farmer preparing small crop beds set around a busy local community market can enrich nutrient-poor topsoil by mixing in well-rotted **compost manure**, **kraal/cattle manure (livestock dung)**, **green manure**, or **decomposed crop residues / leaf mould**.

Organic manures replenish depleted macro-nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) naturally while adding dark **humus**, which glues sandy soil crumbs into spongy aggregates that hold moisture longer between dry spells and feed helpful soil microorganisms and earthworms—giving affordable fertility improvement without costly imported synthetic chemicals.

Always distinguish **organic materials** (**compost, kraal manure, chicken litter, decayed leaves**) from **inorganic commercial fertilisers** (like Compound D or Ammonium Nitrate)—naming an inorganic bag loses the mark when the question specifically asks for *organic* material!

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, b) State one method of controlling weeds.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** Effective methods to control unwanted weeds competing with crops for water, sunlight, and soil nutrients include **mechanical hand-hoeing or shallow hand-pulling before weeds set seed**, **spreading thick organic mulch** between crop rows to smother germinating weed seedlings by blocking sunlight, and practising **crop rotation**.

Timing weed removal early (within the first 2–5 weeks after maize or vegetable emergence) prevents deep weed roots from stealing scarce rainfall and basal fertiliser, while digging out perennial runners cleanly before flowering prevents thousands of fresh weed seeds from dropping into the soil for next season. On Grade 7 gardens, non-chemical mulching and hoeing also protect young tender seedlings and earthworms safely.

ZIMSEC marking guides accept **hand weeding / hoeing**, **mulching**, **crop rotation**, or **appropriate selective herbicide use**—always state a clear active method and briefly link it to cutting competition or preventing seeding.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, c) Explain why maintaining soil fertility is important.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [3 marks]:** Maintaining high **soil fertility** is vital because crops require balanced reserves of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and organic matter to produce **vigorous green leaves, strong root systems, and heavy grain or vegetable yields** year after year. When soil nutrients become exhausted without replenishment, plants turn yellow (chlorotic), stunt badly, resist pests poorly, and leave households short of food and farm income.

From an environmental conservation standpoint, fertile, humus-rich soil retains moisture far better against droughts and resists wind and sheet erosion, allowing farmers to feed families permanently on existing cultivated fields instead of clearing fragile virgin woodlands every few years (*shifting cultivation*).

Be sure to connect fertile soil to **sustainable high crop yields / household food security** AND **long-term land preservation** so your explanation satisfies Paper 2 depth.

questions.questionText: A local market has become untidy after a busy trading day. A learner leaves an ice cube on a plate in a warm classroom and observes water forming around it. a) Name the change taking place as the ice becomes liquid.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** When a solid ice cube absorbs heat energy from warm classroom air set around a busy local community market and turns into liquid water, the physical change of state taking place is called **melting** (physically, fusion from solid to liquid).

At room temperature above **0 °C** (the melting point of pure ice), heat energy transferred from the surrounding warm air breaks apart the rigid, closely packed crystal lattice holding ice molecules still, allowing water particles to slide freely past one another as liquid water while keeping their exact H₂O chemical identity unchanged.

In Grade 7 Science & General Paper, name the exact state-change verb **melting** clearly (do NOT say "dissolving"—salt dissolves in water, whereas ice **melts** purely through heat gain!).

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, b) State what happens to the water if it is cooled enough.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** If that liquid water is cooled down sufficiently (to **0 °C** or below inside a freezer), it loses heat energy to its surroundings and changes back into **solid ice** through the physical change of state called **freezing (solidification)**.

As temperature falls to 0 °C, liquid water molecules slow down until attractive forces lock them neatly back into rigid crystal patterns—expanding slightly as solid ice floats on water. No new chemical substance is produced; only particle energy and arrangement alter.

State both the resulting state (**turns back into solid ice**) and the exact scientific process term (**freezing / solidification at 0 °C**) to guarantee full marks effortlessly.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, c) Explain why this is called a reversible change.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [3 marks]:** Melting and freezing water are called **reversible physical changes** because **no new chemical substance is created during heating or cooling, and the original solid ice can be recovered completely simply by reversing the temperature** (cooling liquid water back to 0 °C turns it straight back into solid ice again).

Unlike **irreversible chemical changes**—such as burning firewood to ash, cooking an egg, or rusting an iron nail, where original materials can never be restored—changes of state (melting, freezing, evaporation, and condensation) rearrange how identical H₂O molecules sit without altering their internal bonds, keeping total mass completely conserved.

ZIMSEC markers look explicitly for **two halves** in every definition of a reversible change: (1) **can be undone / turned back to original form**, and (2) **no new chemical substance is formed**. Including an everyday contrast like *burning wood* makes the explanation crystal clear.

questions.questionText: A local market has become untidy after a busy trading day. A group of learners must cross a busy road on their way home. There is a marked crossing a short distance away. a) State the safest place for them to cross.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** The safest place for learners returning home set around a busy local community market to cross a busy street is directly **at the designated marked pedestrian crossing—specifically a zebra crossing, pelican traffic-light crossing, or footbridge/warden-controlled school crossing**.

Motorists are legally required and visually alerted by white stripes, flashing beacons, and road warning signs to slow down and yield right-of-way to pedestrians at marked crossings, whereas darting across blind corners, highway bends, or gaps between parked buses hides small children from oncoming drivers until braking distance is too short to prevent tragedy.

Give the exact safety infrastructure name from the prompt (**the marked pedestrian / zebra crossing**) directly rather than saying *"anywhere with fewer cars"*.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, b) Give one precaution they should take before crossing.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** Before stepping onto even a marked pedestrian crossing, learners must **stop cleanly on the pavement edge, put phones/earphones away, and follow the Kerb Drill: look right, look left, and look right again (plus listen carefully for horns or approaching engines)**—stepping off only once drivers in all lanes have visibly slowed and halted completely.

Because distracted or speeding drivers occasionally fail to obey zebra stripes in time, making direct **eye contact with drivers** and watching both lanes continuously while walking straight across ensures a pedestrian never walks into an overtaking vehicle hidden behind a stationary bus.

State the structured **Stop → Look right, Look left, Look right again → Walk briskly (never assume cars will stop)** routine clearly for guaranteed marks.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, c) Explain why running across a busy road is dangerous.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [3 marks]:** Running across a busy road is extremely dangerous because **a runner may trip, stumble, or drop schoolbooks directly in front of oncoming traffic, while moving too fast leaves neither the child nor approaching drivers adequate reaction and braking time to avoid a fatal collision**.

Drivers judging gaps expect steady predictable walking speeds; sudden sprinting from behind parked vehicles or across curves prevents high-speed cars and heavy commuter kombis from stopping within safe braking distances—particularly on wet tarmac roads where tyres lose grip. Walking briskly in a straight perpendicular line after confirming clear lanes gives full control and visibility at all times.

Highlight **risk of falling/stumbling** + **reduced reaction/braking time for drivers** cleanly to secure full Paper 2 marks.

questions.questionText: A local market has become untidy after a busy trading day. The school is organising a cultural performance. Learners will combine singing, drumming, movement and visual decoration. a) Name one percussion instrument suitable for the performance.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** An authentic Zimbabwean **percussion instrument** ideal for a school cultural performance set around a busy local community market is the traditional **ngoma (wooden skin drum)** or **hosho (calabash gourd rattles filled with hard *hota* seeds)** (other strong traditional examples include **makwa** wooden clappers, **marimba** xylophones, or **magavu** leg rattles).

Percussion instruments produce sound when struck, shaken, or scraped, laying down rich rhythmic pulse patterns that synchronise singers and traditional dancers (*mbakumba*, *muchongoyo*, *dinhe*, or *amabhiza*) while reflecting proud local craftsmanship carved from indigenous timber and dried gourds.

Ensure you name a genuine **percussion instrument** (struck/shaken—e.g. **ngoma drum, hosho, or marimba**) rather than wind instruments like flutes/whistles or plucked lamellophones/strings if strictly asking for percussion.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, b) State one reason rehearsals are important.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** Regular pre-event **rehearsals** are essential because **they help performers memorise songs, steps, cues, and timing together while spotting and fixing tempo, spacing, or costume problems well before the live audience arrives**.

Practising consistently transforms nervous individual beginners into a smooth, confident ensemble where drummers maintain a steady beat, singers project voices clearly, and dancers hold symmetrical stage lines without bumping into one another or forgetting entries on performance day.

Focus on **practising coordination/timing, memorising routines, correcting mistakes early, and building stage confidence** cleanly in one crisp answer.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, c) Explain how teamwork can improve the performance.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [3 marks]:** Strong **teamwork** elevates a cultural arts showcase because **singers, drummers, dancers, and stage decorators listen closely and coordinate their timing, cues, and energy as one unified group—making rhythms crisp, movements synchronised, and costumes neatly arranged on stage**.

Equally important, supportive teamwork encourages shy peers to step forward confidently, prevents disputes over leadership or props during busy transitions, and splits practical chores (setting backdrop banners, carrying drums, and keeping instruments safe afterward) fairly—embodying Zimbabwe’s communal spirit of *Unhu/Ubuntu*.

Connect **musical/choreographic synchronisation** directly with **mutual support and shared stage responsibility** for top ZIMSEC marks.

**Model Answer [2 marks]:** An authentic Zimbabwean **percussion instrument** ideal for a school cultural performance focused on a school committee environmental improvement plan is the traditional **ngoma (wooden skin drum)** or **hosho (calabash gourd rattles filled with hard *hota* seeds)** (other strong traditional examples include **makwa** wooden clappers, **marimba** xylophones, or **magavu** leg rattles).

Percussion instruments produce sound when struck, shaken, or scraped, laying down rich rhythmic pulse patterns that synchronise singers and traditional dancers (*mbakumba*, *muchongoyo*, *dinhe*, or *amabhiza*) while reflecting proud local craftsmanship carved from indigenous timber and dried gourds.

Ensure you name a genuine **percussion instrument** (struck/shaken—e.g. **ngoma drum, hosho, or marimba**) rather than wind instruments like flutes/whistles or plucked lamellophones/strings if strictly asking for percussion.

questions.questionText: A local market has become untidy after a busy trading day. Learners are discussing how young citizens can care for their school and community. a) State one responsibility of a learner as a member of the school community.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** One vital civic responsibility of every learner as a member of the school community set around a busy local community market is **looking after shared school furniture, books, and cleanliness by placing litter in bins and reporting broken taps or desks—while respecting teachers, following school rules, and treating peers kindly without bullying**.

Citizenship in Primary Social Science pairs **rights** (such as the right to learn safely in clean classrooms) directly with matching **responsibilities**: protecting quiet study time, helping younger learners stay safe on the playground, and participating positively in school clean-up days.

Give an actionable positive duty (**obeying school rules, caring for property, keeping surroundings clean, or respecting others**) framed clearly as a learner’s civic contribution.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, b) Give one example of public property.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [2 marks]:** Classic everyday examples of **public property** built or funded for shared community benefit include **a community borehole or tap, a public primary school classroom/desk, a rural health clinic, a library, public roads/bridges, or municipal parks and bus shelters**.

Unlike private personal property (your own shoes, school satchel, or family bicycle owned exclusively by one household), public property belongs collectively to every resident and is paid for out of shared taxes, community labour, and donor funds so children and families everywhere can access water, healthcare, and education reliably.

State one unmistakable shared community facility (**a public clinic, community borehole, school building, or tarred road/streetlights**) rather than private household items.

questions.questionText: Considering the same situation, c) Explain why public property should be protected.
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [3 marks]:** Protecting **public property** is essential because **repairing vandalised boreholes, stolen solar panels, or broken school desks drains scarce community money that should instead buy medicines, textbooks, and new classrooms—and damaged facilities deprive hundreds of innocent families and learners of vital daily services**.

Respecting public assets demonstrates mature **citizenship and *Unhu/Ubuntu*** stewardship: caring for shared schools and clinics ensures they remain clean, safe, and usable not only today, but also for younger siblings and future generations entering Grade 1 tomorrow.

Tie protection convincingly to **avoiding costly repairs/replacement**, **keeping essential services running for everyone**, and **preserving shared community assets for the future**.
